docs.title: Fritz! exporter for prometheus
docs.text:
This is a prometheus exporter for AVM Fritz! home network devices commonly found in Europe. This exporter uses the devices builtin TR-064 API via the fritzconnection python module.

The exporter should work with Fritz!Box and Fritz!Repeater Devices (and maybe others). It actively checks for supported metrics and queries the metrics for all devices configured (Yes, it has multi-device support for all you Mesh users out there.)

It has been tested against an AVM Fritz!Box 7590 (DSL), a Fritz!Box 5690 (fibre), a Fritz!Box 5530 Fiber, a Fritz!Box 6660 Cable (DOCSIS, FRITZ!OS 8.25), a Fritz!Repeater 2400 and a Fritz!WLAN Repeater 1750E. If you have another box and data is missing, please file an issue or PR on GitHub.

Prometheus required

As the scope of this exporter lies on a typical home device, this also means that there are a lot of people interested in it, who may not have had any contact with Prometheus. As a result of this there have been some misunderstandings in the past, how this all works.

To avoid frustration you will need to know this:

You must setup and configure Prometheus separately! If you are running in plain docker or docker-compose there is a docker-compose setup for Prometheus at https://github.com/vegasbrianc/prometheus which also includes Grafana to actually produce dashboards. This may work out of the box or can be used as a starting point.

The whole setup required is:

  • fritz_exporter: connects to your Fritz device, reads the metrics and makes them available in a format Prometheus understands
  • prometheus: connects to the exporter at regular time intervals, reads the data and stores it in its database
  • grafana: connects to prometheus and can query the database of metrics for timeseries and create dashboards from it.

Check out the Quickstart, which will bring up a simple and limited Prometheus, Grafana and exporter setup.

You cannot connect grafana to the exporter directly. This will not work.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
The following groups of metrics are currently available:

  • Base Information (uptime; model and Fritz!OS version in fritz_device_info)
  • Software Information (update available; its version in fritz_update_info)
  • Connection mode (DSL, fibre, cable, mobile fallback or offline; the access type in fritz_wan_access_type_info)
  • Host table (number of known devices; with host_info enabled, activity and speed of each host by MAC address, and its address, name and connection in fritz_host_info)
  • LAN statistics (Ethernet only)
  • WAN statistics (including the delegated IPv6 prefix)
  • DSL statistics
  • Fibre / GPON statistics (optical levels, SFP/GPON identity, fibre counters)
  • PPP statistics
  • WiFi statistics per band, with SSID and standard in fritz_wifi_info (with wifi_client_info enabled, also signal strength and speed of each client, with band and address in fritz_wifi_client_info)
  • Mesh backhaul links (data rate and state of the links between mesh nodes, read from the mesh master)
  • Provider management channel (TR-069 management server host, periodic inform, managed upgrades; USP controller enable flags, see below)
  • Telephony (number of configured telephone numbers; the numbers themselves are not exported)
  • WAN Layer1 (physical link) statistics, including 64-bit max bitrate for multi-gig links
  • DOCSIS cable channel statistics (auto-detected on cable boxes; power, MER/MSE, corrected/uncorrected errors, latency). On the Fritz!Box 6660 Cable, DOCSIS 3.1 channels report an uncorrected-error counter but no corrected one, so fritz_docsis_corrected_errors_total has no series for them.
  • Shared segment utilization (fritz_cable_segment_*, cable boxes; other boxes report no samples) and per-connection IPv4/IPv6 status, uptime, state and address (fritz_wan_connection_info) via the Fritz!OS REST API
  • Home Automation Devices (switches, heating valves, temperatures, power meters, and battery status; window/door sensors (open/closed) are not yet reported)

docs.title: USP controllers
docs.text:
USP (User Services Platform, Broadband Forum TR-369) is a protocol that lets a remote party read and change settings of a device. Such a party is called a controller. Fritz!OS 8 lists the configured controllers in the TR-064 service X_AVM-DE_USPController1. When a controller is enabled, the box opens an outgoing connection to it and accepts its management commands.

  • fritz_usp_controller_enabled is 1 when the controller with the given index is enabled and 0 when it is configured but switched off.
  • fritz_usp_myfritz_enabled is 1 when the MyFRITZ controller (AVM's cloud service) is enabled.

On a FRITZ!Box 6660 Cable running FRITZ!OS 8.25 there is one controller, the MyFRITZ service, and both values are 0. The metrics are meant for alerting: a value switching to 1 means a remote party has been allowed to manage the box, which you would only expect after you (or your provider) changed that on purpose. The exporter only reports the flags. Endpoint IDs, host names and credentials are never read or exported.

docs.title: Exporter self-monitoring
docs.text:
In addition to the Fritz device data above, the exporter reports metrics about its own operation:

  • fritz_device_reachable -- whether a device was reachable during the last scrape (labelled by friendly_name only)
  • fritz_scrapes_total -- number of completed scrape cycles per device
  • fritz_scrapes_timeouts_total -- scrapes skipped because a previous scrape was still in progress when the collector lock deadline was reached
  • fritz_scrapes_failed_total -- scrapes aborted by an unexpected error
  • fritz_read_problem -- 1 while the exporter skips data of a capability (labels capability and level): partial (some values or items could not be read), skipped (the whole capability), or error (a bug in the exporter, please report it). capability="ConnectionMode" stands for the fritz_connection_mode metric. The series disappears when the problem is gone, and is not exported while the device is unreachable. Use it to explain gaps in other metrics, or to alert on them; the log has the details: a warning when a problem appears, an hourly reminder while it lasts (with the time it started) and an info line when it is gone.

The standard prometheus_client process and interpreter metrics (process_*, python_gc_*, python_info) are exposed as well.

If there is any information missing or not displayed on your specific device, please open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: Event log
docs.text: The exporter reads metrics, not the device's event log ("Ereignisse"). For that there is a companion tool, fritz_logextractor (documentation): it reads the event log and writes each new entry once as a JSON line, so a log stack such as Loki or Elasticsearch can keep it across reboots of the box. It brings a Grafana dashboard and example configs for common log collectors.

docs.title: Known Problems
docs.text:
• It seems like Fritz!OS does not internally count the packets for the Guest WiFi. So even though those counters are there they are always 0. This seems to be a problem with Fritz!OS and not the exporter. The counters are delivered nontheless, just in case this gets fixed by AVM.
  • On multi-gig fibre (and possibly cable) links the classic fritz_wan_max_bitrate values from GetCommonLinkProperties can be wrong (often stuck at 1000000) because they use a 32-bit field. Prefer fritz_wan_layer1_max_bitrate_bps from GetAddonInfos, which correctly reports e.g. 2.5 Gbit/s / 1.25 Gbit/s.
  • On WAN types that don't support the 64-bit Layer1 max bitrate fields (observed on cable), FRITZ!OS reports NewX_AVM_DE_Layer1DownstreamMaxBitRate64 / NewX_AVM_DE_Layer1UpstreamMaxBitRate64 as an empty string rather than omitting them or returning None. The exporter treats this the same as "not provided" and simply omits fritz_wan_layer1_max_bitrate_bps for that direction/device — it does not indicate a fault, only that this WAN type doesn't expose the field.
  • Fibre / X_AVM-DE_WANFiber gaps observed on FRITZ!Box 5690 (Fritz!OS 8.25): the web UI shows real optical readings, but several TR-064 GetInfo / GetStatistics fields are empty or zero. The exporter still exposes the TR-064 values when present. The Fritz! team has been contacted about these issues:
    • NewOpticalSignalLevel / NewTransmitOpticalLevel stay at 0 while the UI shows real RX/TX power (e.g. about -19.5 dBm / 2.4 dBm). Also seen on a FRITZ!Box 5530 Fiber. When TR-064 reports 0 for both, the exporter reads fritz_fiber_optical_signal_level and fritz_fiber_transmit_optical_level from the web UI page the UI itself uses (data.lua?page=fiberStats). That page holds one value per hour, so these two metrics then change only once an hour and can lag up to an hour behind the link: after a fibre outage they may still show the last good level for that long.
    • NewFiberMode stays at Unknown while the UI reports GPON (ITU G.984)
    • SFP metadata (NewSFPVendor, NewSFPPartNumber, NewSFPSerialNumber, NewSFPType) is empty
    • no TR-064 field for RX wavelength (UI shows 1490 nm; only NewTXWaveLength exists)
    • laser temperature and laser supply voltage exist only in the web UI, not in TR-064
    • GetStatistics RX counters (NewBytesReceived / NewPacketsReceived) and NewConnectionRateDown often stay at 0 while TX side is populated
  • If you receive Fatal Python error: init_interp_main: can't initialize time when running the container you may have to update libseccomp on your Docker host. This issue mainly happens on Raspberry Pi and is triggered by a version of libseccomp2 which is too old. See https://askubuntu.com/questions/1263284/apt-update-throws-signature-error-in-ubuntu-20-04-container-on-arm (Method 2) and https://github.com/pdreker/fritz_exporter/issues/38.
  • On some boxes LAN Packet counters are stuck at 0 even though the box reports the stats as available.
  • Fritz!OS does not allow passwords longer than 32 characters (as of 07.25). If you try to use a longer password, the admin ui will simply discard all characters after the 32nd. The UI will also cut your inserted password down to 32 characters. So you will be able to login in the UI with the long password. The exporter however does not alter your password and requests will result in a 401 Unauthorized error. So please be aware of this limit and choose a suitable password.
  • Collecting HostInfo (disabled by default) can be extremely slow and will cause some load on the device. It works, but it is slow as this feature needs two calls to the Fritz! device for every device it knows which will simply take some time. If you enable this, make sure your Prometheusm scrape_timeouts are set appropriately (30s should be OK for most setups, but you may need to go even higher).

docs.title: Grafana Dashboards
docs.text:
Two Grafana dashboards come with the exporter, in misc/grafana in the repository. Take them from the tag of the exporter version you run, so they match its metrics, e.g. https://github.com/pdreker/fritz_exporter/tree/fritzexporter-v4.0.0/misc/grafana for 4.0.0; main has the dashboards of the next release. Import them with "Dashboards" -> "New" -> "Import" -> "Upload dashboard JSON file" in Grafana 10 or later, and pick your Prometheus data source and the device at the top.

  • Fritz!Exporter Overview (fritz-exporter-overview.json) shows every metric the exporter has, one row per topic (device, internet, DSL, cable, fibre, LAN, WiFi, mesh, hosts, smart home, provider management), with many kinds of panels. Use it to see what there is and as a starting point for your own dashboards. Rows that do not apply to a device stay empty.
  • Fritz!Exporter Home (fritz-exporter-home.json) shows what is useful every day on one screen: connection, traffic, line usage and quality, devices online, WiFi, mesh and smart home.

Hosts need host_info: true and WiFi clients wifi_client_info: true.

docs.title: Helm Chart
docs.text: There is a (rather crude) Helm chart under helm in the repository. It will deploy the exporter and also create a service monitor for Prometheus Operator to automatically scrape the exporter.

docs.title: Helping out
docs.text:
If your device delivers some metrics which are not yet scraped by this exporter you can either create a Pull Request, which will be gladly accepted ;-)

Alternatively you can use the following commands and the little helper script in the root of this repository to let me know of metrics:

fritzconnection -i <FRITZ-IP> -s # Lists available services
fritzconnection -i <FRITZ-IP> -S <ServiceName> # Lists available action for a service
python -m fritz_export_helper <FRITZ-IP> <USERNAME> <PASSWORD> -s <ServiceName> -a <ActionName> # Will output the data returned from the device in a readable format

If you have found something you need/want, open an issue provide the following infos:

  1. Model of Device (e.g. FritzBox DSL 7590)
  2. ServiceName and ActionName
  3. Output from fritz_export_helper (make sure, there is not secret data, like password or WiFi passwords in there, before sending!)
  4. What output you need/want and a little bit of info of the environment (Cable, DSL, Hybrid LTE Mode, ... whatever might be relevant)

docs.title: Building
docs.text: The recommended way to run this exporter is from a Docker container. The included Dockerfile builds the exporter using a Python:alpine base image and produces a clean, minimal runtime image.

docs.title: Building and running from a local image
docs.text:
To build clone the repository from GitHub, enter the repository and execute

docker build -t fritz_exporter:local .

from inside the source directory.

To run the resulting image use

docker run -d --name fritz_exporter -p <PORT>:<FRITZ_EXPORTER_PORT> -e FRITZ_EXPORTER_CONFIG="192.168.178.1,username,password" fritz_exporter:local

docs.title: Verify correct operation
docs.text:
To verify correct operation just use curl against the running exporter. It should reply with a Prometheus-style list of metrics:

> curl localhost:<FRITZ_EXPORTER_PORT>

# HELP python_gc_objects_collected_total Objects collected during gc
# TYPE python_gc_objects_collected_total counter
python_gc_objects_collected_total{generation="0"} 481.0
python_gc_objects_collected_total{generation="1"} 112.0
python_gc_objects_collected_total{generation="2"} 0.0
# HELP python_gc_objects_uncollectable_total Uncollectable object found during GC
# TYPE python_gc_objects_uncollectable_total counter
python_gc_objects_uncollectable_total{generation="0"} 0.0
python_gc_objects_uncollectable_total{generation="1"} 0.0
python_gc_objects_uncollectable_total{generation="2"} 0.0
...

Note

If you have the host_info config enabled for one or more devices please be aware, that it may take a long time to receive the reply, as the metrics are read sequentially when queried. Practical experience has shown that a device knowing around 70 WiFi devices may take 20-30s to reply to all metrics queries. So set appropriate timeouts.

docs.title: Building and running locally (no containers)
docs.text:
You can install the latest release from PyPI using pip install fritz-exporter and then run it using python -m fritzexporter. It is highly recommended to use a virtual environment to do so.

For development and debugging, see Contributing for the local environment setup, verification commands, and how to run the exporter from source.

docs.title: General structure
docs.text: fritz_exporter uses some "black magic" (this may be clever, but it makes understanding what's going on a lot harder...) to manage capabilities of devices. This section will try to make some sense of this code... At least for the author...

docs.title: Module / File Map
docs.text:
A quick orientation before diving in:

fritzexporter/
  __main__.py           – CLI entry point and main loop (parse_cmdline, main)
  fritzdevice.py        – FritzDevice, FritzCollector, DeviceSpec, FritzCredentials
  fritzcapabilities.py  – FritzCapability (ABC) + all concrete capability classes
                          + FritzCapabilities container
  reply.py              – Typed reading of device replies (Reply, read_action,
                          Issues, DataError), see "Reading Device Data"
  tr064_remote.py       – TR-064 connection setup: ports, TLS, timeouts, the
                          /tr064 prefix for WAN remote access
  fritz_webui.py        – Web interface client: login, data.lua, REST API, AHA
  fritz_aha.py          – Parser for the AHA (smart home) device list XML
  fritz_docsis.py       – Parser for the DOCSIS cable channel page (docInfo)
  fritz_fiber.py        – Parser for the fibre optical level page (fiberStats)
  fritz_rest_generic.py – Parsers for REST API connections and segment monitor
  exceptions.py         – Top-level exceptions
  config/
    config.py           – ExporterConfig, DeviceConfig (attrs @define classes)
                          + get_config() factory
    exceptions.py       – Config-specific exceptions

docs.title: Startup Flow
docs.text:
The entry point is fritzexporter/__main__.py → main().

  1. A FritzCollector is created (empty, no devices yet).
  2. Configuration is loaded via get_config(), which reads either a YAML file or environment variables and returns an ExporterConfig instance.
  3. For each DeviceConfig in the config, _register_device() builds a DeviceSpec (credentials, name, options) and hands it to fritzcollector.add_device(), the one place where devices are set up. It instantiates a FritzDevice, which connects to the physical device via fritzconnection, reads its serial number and model, and probes which capabilities it supports (see below).
  4. A device that was set up is registered. A device that could not be set up — unreachable, wrong credentials, no capabilities, or no readable serial number — is kept as an OfflineDevice with its DeviceSpec instead, logged once without a traceback: it is reported as fritz_device_reachable 0 and set up again in the background, started by each scrape, until it works. A device that answers but gives no readable serial number is given up after SERIAL_RETRIES (3) retries, with an error in the log; it stays reported as unreachable until the exporter is restarted. A warning is logged whenever the reason an offline device fails changes.
  5. The FritzCollector is registered with the Prometheus REGISTRY. Its describe() returns nothing, so registering does not run a scrape to learn the metric names.
  6. An HTTP server is started (prometheus_client.start_http_server), and the main thread waits forever; scrapes run in the HTTP server's threads.

When Prometheus scrapes /metrics, FritzCollector.collect() is called. It holds a re-entrant lock (threading.RLock) for the whole scrape, so concurrent scrapes do not interfere. A scrape that cannot get the lock within SCRAPE_LOCK_TIMEOUT (30 s) returns no data and is counted in fritz_scrapes_timeouts_total. Offline devices are set up again in one background thread (fritz-offline-retry), which a scrape starts unless it is still running; the scrape does not wait for it, so a device that takes its connection timeout to fail holds up no scrape.

docs.title: Configuration System
docs.text:
config/config.py provides two attrs @define classes:

DeviceConfig Represents one Fritz! device. Fields: hostname, username, password, password_file, name, host_info, wifi_client_info, connection_timeout, use_tls, port, remote_access, allow_unsafe_md5_password. Hostname is lowercased automatically via an attrs converter, and the name defaults to it. Validators check that a password or password file is given, password length, that any password file actually exists, the port range, and that remote_access is only set together with use_tls.

ExporterConfig Top-level exporter configuration. Fields: exporter_port (default 9787), log_level, listen_address, devices (list of DeviceConfig).

get_config(path) delegates to either _read_config_file() (YAML) or _read_config_from_env() (environment variables) and then calls ExporterConfig.from_config(raw_dict). Both paths hand on only the keys that are set, so the defaults live in one place, the field definitions. from_config refuses keys the class has no field for, and duplicate device names.

Both config classes use attrs validators and converters — field values are validated and coerced at construction time. Every config problem raises a ConfigError (config/exceptions.py) whose message names the device and the key; main() logs it as one line and exits.

docs.title: The Capability System
docs.text:
This is the "black magic" part. Read carefully.

Auto-registration of subclasses

FritzCapability is an abstract base class (ABC) defined in fritzcapabilities.py. Every concrete capability (e.g. DeviceInfo, WanDSLInterfaceConfig) is a subclass of it. The __init_subclass__ hook fires automatically when Python loads each subclass definition and appends the new class to the class-level list FritzCapability.subclasses. This means no manual registration is needed — just define the subclass and it is discovered automatically.

FritzCapabilities (plural) — the container

FritzCapabilities is a dict-like wrapper around {class_name: instance} for every known FritzCapability subclass. It can be constructed in two modes:

  • Without a device — instantiates all subclasses but leaves every instance's present flag as False. Used by FritzCollector to drive the collect loop and hold the metric families.
  • With a device — same construction, then immediately calls check_present() which runs check_capability() on every instance against that specific device.

Capability probing (check_capability)

FritzCapability.check_capability(device) performs a two-stage check:

  1. Static check: each capability declares a self.requirements list of (service, action) tuples. The method verifies that each service exists in device.fc.services and that the action is listed in that service's actions dict.
  2. Live call check: even if the static check passes, some Fritz! devices advertise services they do not actually support. The method therefore tries to call each requirement and, if FritzServiceError, FritzActionError, or similar exceptions are raised, it marks the capability present = False again.

Some capabilities replace this check: HostInfo and WlanAssociatedDevices are only present when enabled in the device config (host_info, wifi_client_info), WanDocsisCable is detected by the WAN access type, and WlanConfigurationInfo checks each WLAN band on its own.

The present flag of each FritzCapability instance reflects whether that device supports that capability.

The collect loop

When FritzCollector.collect() runs:

  1. The background retry of offline devices is started, unless it is still running or every offline device was given up. Devices that the previous retry set up are registered now, so they are collected one scrape after they come back.
  2. FritzDevice.add_connection_mode() adds each device's sample to one fritz_connection_mode gauge (DSL/fibre/mobile/cable/offline).
  3. The collector holds its own FritzCapabilities instance, built without a device: one instance of every capability class, used only to drive the loop and to hold the metric families. For each capability capa in it, capa.get_metrics(devices, name) is called:
    1. capa.create_metrics() re-creates the Prometheus metric families, clearing the values of the previous scrape.
    2. It iterates over every registered device and calls capa._generate_metric_values(device) only when device.capabilities[name].present is True for that device. Each call is guarded, see Reading Device Data below.
    3. capa._get_metric_values() yields all its metric families (self.metrics).
  4. The self-monitoring metrics follow: fritz_scrapes_total, fritz_scrapes_timeouts_total, fritz_scrapes_failed_total, fritz_device_reachable and fritz_read_problem.

All device data is collected before anything is yielded, so the availability reported in fritz_device_reachable matches the data of the same scrape.

The indirection — one capability instance per class drives the loop, the per-device capability flags decide whether values are fetched — is the key to understanding the flow.

docs.title: tl;dr
docs.text:
FritzCollector has a list of FritzDevices and its own FritzCapabilities collection with one instance of every capability class.

Each FritzDevice has its own FritzCapabilities collection recording which capabilities that device actually supports (and, per capability, the current read problem, see below).

During collect(), the collector's set drives iteration; the per-device sets gate whether values are fetched from each device.

docs.title: Reading Device Data
docs.text:
Every value taken from a device — a TR-064 action result, a data.lua or REST API JSON object, an element of the AHA XML — is read through fritzexporter/reply.py, never by indexing the raw data:

  • read_action(device, service, action, **arguments) calls a TR-064 action and returns a Reply, a read-only typed view on the result. Reply(raw, source) wraps a JSON object the same way.
  • reply.num(key), reply.integer(key), reply.flag(key) and reply.text(key, default) read a required value; the opt_* variants return None instead. reply.opt_obj(key) and reply.items(key) read nested objects and lists; issues.objects(reply, key) walks a list of objects. to_float/to_int/to_bool/to_str do the same for single values, e.g. list items or XML text.

One rule applies everywhere: a value that is missing, None, "", [] or {} is absent (empty containers, because JSON encoders for Lua — which the web interface is written in — send an empty list as {} and vice versa) (required reads raise, optional reads return None); a value that is present but not of the requested type raises DataError. Numbers come back as int/float and labels as str. A DataError names the source and field, never the value.

docs.title: Failures stay at the level they affect
docs.text:
A failure should cost only what depends on it, and must move up a level when that level depends on it. Prometheus handles gaps; the exporter logs each one, so a gap in a graph can be matched to a log line.

Level Example Effect Value the MER of one DOCSIS channel is "abc" only the samples built from it Item a host, channel or WLAN band has an unreadable label only that item Capability the reply is not an object, a list is not a list, or a value the whole capability depends on that capability of that device in this scrape (no partial set) Capability a bug in the exporter (KeyError, TypeError, ...) as above, logged with a traceback on every scrape Device the device answers, but its serial number cannot be read registered offline; given up after SERIAL_RETRIES (3) retries Capability the device answers a TR-064 request with an error (FritzActionError, ...) that capability of that device in this scrape Device the device does not answer (tr064_remote.TRANSPORT_ERRORS) unreachable for this scrape

How the levels are built:

  • Value: read through the Issues collector of the capability, self.issues: self.issues.num(reply, key), opt_num, num_or, opt_integer, flag, equals, text, convert. They behave like the Reply methods but record a DataError and return None; self._add(metric, labels, value) adds no sample for None.
  • Item: wrap the item in with self._item("host 3"): (in a capability) or with issues.item(...) (in a parser). A DataError inside skips the rest of the block and drops the samples it already added. issues.objects(reply, key) skips list elements that are no objects.
  • Capability: anything read strictly (reply.num(), reply.text() without self.issues) outside an item. Read a value strictly when the capability depends on it, e.g. a label shared by all its samples or a count that drives a loop.
  • Device: FritzDevice.get_device_info raises FritzDeviceSerialUnknownError; the device is not collected, because the serial is the label that tells devices apart (names are unique only among the configured devices).

FritzCapability._collect_device, called by get_metrics for each device, guards its _generate_metric_values call. In every case below, the samples that device added to the capability are dropped, so no partial set is exported:

  • a connection error marks the device unavailable for this scrape;
  • a FritzWebUiError or DataError skips the capability for this scrape;
  • any other error (KeyError, TypeError, ...) is a bug, since all reads go through reply.py: it is contained the same way, so it does not break the scrape, but logged with a traceback on every scrape.

Before samples are kept, they are checked to be renderable (numeric value, str labels), because prometheus_client converts values only while rendering the scrape.

Reporting. Each device and capability keeps its current problem level (partial, skipped or error):

  • fritz_read_problem{capability, level} is 1 while a problem lasts, so a gap in a graph can be explained from Prometheus alone, even weeks later. It is exported only for reachable devices (for the others, nothing was read). get_connection_mode reports its problems the same way, as capability="ConnectionMode"; report_problem() does the bookkeeping for both;
  • a warning is logged when a problem appears or changes level, a reminder with the start time every hour (PROBLEM_REMINDER_INTERVAL) while it lasts, the details at debug level on the other scrapes, and an info line when it is gone. Comparing the level, not the text, keeps changing item indexes from causing new warnings.

A capability does not catch errors itself, except where it can do better than skip, e.g. when TR-064 answers 0 for both fibre levels, they come from the web interface instead, and a failure there leaves them out but keeps the rest of the fibre data.

docs.title: Adding a New Metric / Capability
docs.text:
1. Open fritzexporter/fritzcapabilities.py.
  2. Create a new subclass of FritzCapability. The name of the class becomes the key used to look up the capability in every FritzCapabilities dict.
  3. In __init__, call super().__init__() and then populate self.requirements with the (service, action) tuples the metric requires. These are TR-064 service/action pairs as exposed by fritzconnection.
  4. Implement create_metrics(self) — create the metric families with self._gauge(key, name, help, *labels, unit=...) for current values and self._counter(...) for monotonically increasing counters; both put the serial and friendly_name labels first. Name new metrics by the Prometheus naming rules (base units as a suffix via unit=, _total for counters, ratios 0–1); existing names are kept as they are for compatibility, even where they predate these rules.
  5. Implement _generate_metric_values(self, device) — call the TR-064 actions via read_action(device, service, action) and add samples with self._add(key, labels, self.issues.num(reply, field)), keeping failures at their level (see Reading Device Data).
  6. If the capability reads the web interface, set uses_webui = True and get the client with self._webui(device); if a config option switches it on, override enabled(device); if a requirement needs arguments to be probed, override _probe(). Tables read by index go through self._enumerate().
  7. Add tests in tests/test_fritzcapabilities.py using the mock infrastructure in tests/fc_services_mock.py; collect_device() in tests/collect.py sets up one fake device and scrapes it. No further registration is needed; the subclass is discovered automatically via __init_subclass__.
  8. Show the new metrics in the overview dashboard, see Grafana Dashboards below.

docs.title: Grafana Dashboards
docs.text:
misc/grafana/build_dashboards.py writes the two dashboards in misc/grafana (classic dashboard JSON, Grafana 10 and later). Edit the script, never the JSON, and run it:

uv run python misc/grafana/build_dashboards.py

tests/test_grafana_dashboards.py fails when the JSON is not what the script writes, when a metric family of the exporter is missing from the overview, when a query does not select the device (friendly_name="$device"), when a query uses a label or label value that the demo exporter's boxes do not send, or when panels overlap.

To look at the dashboards, run Prometheus and Grafana (e.g. in containers) and let Prometheus scrape your exporter and misc/grafana/demo_exporter.py. The demo exporter serves a cable and a fibre box with smart home devices, built from the test fixtures, with values that change over time, so the panels for hardware you do not have show data:

uv run python misc/grafana/demo_exporter.py 9788

docs.title: Supporting Modules
docs.text:
reply.py

Typed reading of every device reply and the Issues collector for the value and item level; see Reading Device Data.

tr064_remote.py

Creates the FritzConnection for a device (create_fritz_connection) from its ConnectionOptions: TR-064 and web interface ports, TLS, the per-request timeout (fritzconnection's own HTTP calls have none), and, for WAN remote access, a session that prefixes TR-064 paths with /tr064.

fritz_webui.py

FritzWebUiClient, the client for everything only the web interface offers: the challenge-response login (PBKDF2; the legacy MD5 login only with allow_unsafe_md5_password), data.lua pages, the /api/v0 REST API and the AHA smart home interface. All requests go through _request, which reads at most MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES (4 MiB) of a reply. Errors are raised as FritzWebUiError with texts that never contain the session id. The client logs in again only when the device rejects the session (HTTP 401/403, or the HTML login page instead of JSON). Once a request finds the device not answering, the other web interface requests of the scrape fail at once (start_scrape() resets this). A device that offers only the MD5 login, which is not allowed for it, gets no web interface requests until the exporter is restarted.

fritz_aha.py, fritz_docsis.py, fritz_fiber.py, fritz_rest_generic.py

Parsers for the web interface replies: the AHA device list (XML, via defusedxml), the DOCSIS channel page, the fibre optical level history and the REST API connection and segment monitor endpoints. Each turns a raw reply into typed data through reply.py and takes an Issues collector, so a defective value or item is skipped and recorded instead of failing the whole capability.

exceptions.py

Defines FritzDeviceHasNoCapabilitiesError, raised when a device is connected successfully but no capabilities are detected, and FritzDeviceSerialUnknownError, raised when its serial number cannot be read. In both cases the device is registered offline. Config-specific exceptions are in config/exceptions.py, web interface exceptions in fritz_webui.py and DataError in reply.py.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The exporter supports two methods of configuration:

  • via environment variable
  • via config file

docs.title: Environment variable
docs.text:
If you only need a single device this is the easiest way to configure the exporter.

Env variable Description Default FRITZ_NAME User-friendly name for the device hostname FRITZ_HOSTNAME Hostname of the device fritz.box FRITZ_USERNAME Username to authenticate on the device none FRITZ_PASSWORD Password to use for authentication none FRITZ_PASSWORD_FILE File to read the password from FRITZ_LISTEN_ADDRESS Address to listen on. Can be IPv4 or IPv6. 127.0.0.1 FRITZ_PORT Listening port for the exporter 9787 FRITZ_LOG_LEVEL Application log level: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL INFO FRITZ_HOST_INFO Enable extended information about all hosts (slow, see the note below). Only "true" or "1" enable it. False FRITZ_WIFI_CLIENT_INFO Enable per-client WiFi metrics (signal/speed). Only "true" or "1" will enable this feature. False FRITZ_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT Per-device connect/read timeout in seconds for TR-064 and the web interface. 0 disables the timeout. 10 FRITZ_USE_TLS Use HTTPS for TR-064 and the web interface. Only true or 1 enable this. The exporter does not verify the certificate (Fritz!Box certs are self-signed). False FRITZ_DEVICE_PORT Optional device port, see Ports, TLS and remote access. Distinct from FRITZ_PORT (exporter listen port). 0 or unset = default. FRITZ_REMOTE_ACCESS Scrape over AVM WAN remote access, see Ports, TLS and remote access. Requires FRITZ_USE_TLS=true. Only true or 1 enable this. False FRITZ_ALLOW_UNSAFE_MD5_PASSWORD Allow the legacy MD5 web login of Fritz!OS before 7.24, see Legacy MD5 web login. Only true or 1 enable this. False

When using the environment vars you can only specify a single device. If you need multiple devices please use the config file.

Example for a device (at 192.168.178.1 username "monitoring" and the password "mysupersecretpassword"):

export FRITZ_NAME='My Fritz!Box'
export FRITZ_HOSTNAME='192.168.178.1'
export FRITZ_USERNAME='monitoring'
export FRITZ_PASSWORD='mysupersecretpassword'

docs.title: Config file
docs.text:
To use the config file you have to specify the location of the config and mount the appropriate file into the container. The location can be specified by using the --config parameter.

# Full example config file for Fritz-Exporter
exporter_port: 9787 # optional
listen_address: 0.0.0.0 # optional; default 127.0.0.1, set 0.0.0.0 in a container
log_level: DEBUG # optional
devices:
- name: Fritz!Box 7590 Router # optional; default: the hostname. Must be unique
  hostname: fritz.box
  username: prometheus
  password: prometheus
  host_info: True # optional, see below
  wifi_client_info: True # optional, per-client WiFi signal/speed (higher cardinality)
  connection_timeout: 10 # optional, seconds; 0 disables timeout (default 10)
  use_tls: false # optional; true = HTTPS for TR-064 and the web interface
  port: 49000 # optional; TR-064 port locally, shared remote port with remote_access
  remote_access: false # optional; true = WAN remote access (requires use_tls)
  allow_unsafe_md5_password: false # optional; true = allow MD5 web login (Fritz!OS < 7.24)
- name: Repeater Wohnzimmer # optional
  hostname: repeater-Wohnzimmer
  username: prometheus
  password_file: /path/to/password.txt

Every device needs password or password_file. The exporter refuses to start on a key it does not know (e.g. pasword:) and on two devices with the same name; the error message names the device and the key.

Note

host_info: true (env: FRITZ_HOST_INFO) collects extended information about every device known to your Fritz device, which can take a long time (20+ seconds). If you want it, set your Prometheus scrape interval and timeout to match.

Note

wifi_client_info: true (env: FRITZ_WIFI_CLIENT_INFO) exposes per-station WiFi metrics (signal strength and negotiated speed) for every associated client, on the box and on mesh repeaters alike. This adds one time series per connected client, so it is disabled by default — enable it only if you want per-client visibility and are aware of the extra cardinality.

docs.title: Ports, TLS and remote access
docs.text:
The exporter talks to two interfaces on the device: TR-064 for most metrics, and the web interface for smart home (AHA), DOCSIS, fibre and REST API metrics. Which ports it uses depends on use_tls, port and remote_access:

Mode TR-064 Web interface Local (default) http, port 49000 http, port 80 Local, use_tls: true https, port 49443 https, port 443 remote_access: true (requires use_tls: true) https, port (default 443), path prefix /tr064 https, port (default 443)

In local mode port sets the TR-064 port only; the web interface stays on 80 or 443.

In remote mode the device serves TR-064 and the web interface on one port: the HTTPS port set for internet access to the device ("Internet > Permit Access > FRITZ!Box Services"). Set hostname to the device's public name (often a MyFRITZ or DynDNS name) and port to that port. LAN scrapes should leave remote access disabled (default).

docs.title: Legacy MD5 web login
docs.text:
Fritz!OS 7.24 and later log in to the web interface with PBKDF2. Older firmware only offers an MD5 login. Anyone who can read the traffic between exporter and device can recover the password from an MD5 login, and on a hostile network can make a newer device ask for one. The exporter therefore refuses the MD5 login by default: when a device asks for it, the exporter logs an error and reads no more web interface metrics (smart home, DOCSIS, fibre, REST API) from that device until it is restarted. Its TR-064 metrics and all other devices keep working; fritz_read_problem{level="skipped"} shows the metric groups left out.

Upgrade Fritz!OS if you can. If you cannot, set allow_unsafe_md5_password: true (env: FRITZ_ALLOW_UNSAFE_MD5_PASSWORD) for that device to accept the risk. The exporter then logs a warning on every MD5 login. TR-064 uses its own login, see Exporter user and password.

docs.title: Exporter user and password
docs.text:
TR-064 logs in with HTTP digest authentication, and Fritz!Box devices only offer it with MD5. Without TLS, anyone who can read one request between exporter and device can try passwords against it offline, fast. Most devices do not offer HTTPS, so the password is what protects the account.

Create a separate user for the exporter, give it only the rights it needs, and set a random password of at least 20 characters (the device allows at most 32). That puts offline guessing out of reach. On a trusted LAN this is little more than good habit; it matters when the traffic crosses networks you do not control.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Thank you for contributing to fritz_exporter. This guide describes the local development environment and the checks that changes must pass before a pull request is opened.

docs.title: Development environment
docs.text:
The project requires Python 3.14 or later and uses uv to manage its virtual environment and dependencies. Clone your fork, then install all development dependency groups from the locked dependency set:

git clone https://github.com/<your-account>/fritz_exporter.git
cd fritz_exporter
uv sync --all-groups

uv creates and manages the project's virtual environment automatically. Run project commands through uv run; do not activate the environment or install dependencies with pip manually.

docs.title: Running locally
docs.text:
To run the exporter from the checked-out source, provide a configuration file or the required environment variables:

uv run python -m fritzexporter --config /path/to/config.yaml

See Configuration for the available configuration options.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Run all four checks before opening or updating a pull request:

uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format --check .
uv run ty check
uv run pytest

These are the same lint, format, type-check, and test commands run by the Run Tests GitHub Actions workflow. pytest collects branch coverage and writes coverage.xml as configured in pyproject.toml.

Use uv run ruff format . to apply formatting fixes. Address Ruff findings in production code rather than disabling rules unless a narrowly scoped noqa is necessary.

docs.title: Managing dependencies
docs.text:
Dependencies and tools are declared in pyproject.toml and locked in uv.lock. Use uv to change them:

uv add <package>
uv remove <package>

Do not edit uv.lock by hand. Run uv sync --all-groups after pulling dependency changes.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
Create a topic branch from main; do not commit directly to main. Name branches <type>/<short-description>, such as fix/timeout-handling or docs/contributing-guide.

Use Conventional Commit messages:

<type>(<optional scope>): <description>

The allowed types are feat, fix, perf, refactor, style, test, build, ops, docs, and merge. Pull requests should include relevant tests and user-facing documentation changes.

docs.title: Docker images
docs.text: Docker images for this exporter are available from Docker Hub. The images are built for amd64, arm6, arm7 and arm8/64, so they should run on almost all relevant platforms (Intel, Raspberry Pi (basically any version) and Apple Silicon).

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: Tag Description develop Latest build from develop branch. This may be unstable and change at any time without notice or regards for compatibility! latest Latest released version. This might automatically upgrade through major releases, which may be incompatible with currently running versions. Can be used, if you don't mind the occasional breakage. Major releases are rare. full version (e.g. 2.1.1) Specific released versions. Will not update your images without you explicity changing the image tag in Docker. major (e.g. "2") Specific major version. E.g. "2" will install any 2.x.y release thus avoiding unexpected major upgrades which may be incompatible or contain breaking changes. Recommended major.minor (e.g. 2.1) Specific major/minor version. E.g. "2.1" will install the latest 2.1.x release thus avoiding unexpected major upgrades which may be incompatible or contain breaking changes. This will effectively only update patch releases.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This Quickstart is intended for users, who have no current Prometheus or Grafana instance running. This will use docker-compose to run the exporter, prometheus and Grafana. This will also require some configuration in Grafana to connect to prometheus.

Note

Please understand that configuring Prometheus and Grafana are not part of this exporter and as such this is just intended to give a quick starting point. Problems with setting up and configuring either Prometheus and Grafana are out of scope for this quickstart. Please refrain from opening issues against this exporter for Prometheus or Grafana problems.

docs.title: Preparations
docs.text:
Create a new user account for the exporter on the Fritzbox using the login credentials FRITZ_USERNAME: 'xxxxx' and FRITZ_PASSWORD: 'xxxx'. Grant the user access to the FRITZ!Box settings. This automaticaly also allows voice messages, fax messages, FRITZ!App Fon and call list, and Smart Home. Use a long random password for it, see Exporter user and password.

Create an empty directory fritz-exporter and place a file docker-compose.yml in that directory with the following content (Check that environment variables and paths match your setup):

services:
  fritz-exporter:
    image: pdreker/fritz_exporter:4
    container_name: fritz-exporter
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      FRITZ_HOSTNAME: '192.168.178.1'
      FRITZ_USERNAME: 'xxxxx'
      FRITZ_PASSWORD: 'xxxx'
    ports:
      - "9787:9787"

  prometheus:
    container_name: prometheus
    image: prom/prometheus:v3
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus/:/etc/prometheus/
    ports:
      - 9090:9090

  grafana:
    container_name: grafana
    image: grafana/grafana:13.1
    ports:
      - 3000:3000

Create another empty directory prometheus next to the docker-compose.yml file and put a file prometheus.yml into it with the following content:

global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
  evaluation_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "fritz-exporter"
    scrape_interval: 60s
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["fritz-exporter:9787"]

Next run docker compose up -d which should start the 3 services. Use docker ps -a to check, that all containers are actually running.

❯ docker ps -a
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE                           COMMAND                  CREATED         STATUS         PORTS                    NAMES
2bb64e672ddf   prom/prometheus:v3              "/bin/prometheus --c…"   3 seconds ago   Up 2 seconds   0.0.0.0:9090->9090/tcp   prometheus
3b4a78035327   pdreker/fritz_exporter:4        "python -m fritzexpo…"   3 seconds ago   Up 2 seconds   0.0.0.0:9787->9787/tcp   fritz-exporter
9c7473367721   grafana/grafana:13.1            "/run.sh"                3 seconds ago   Up 2 seconds   0.0.0.0:3000->3000/tcp   grafana

docs.title: Checking Prometheus
docs.text:
Point your browser to http://localhost:9090/targets to access the prometheus UI and navigate to Status -> Targets. You should see the fritz-exporter Target (the exporter) being Up. If the Last Scrape Column says "never", wait for a minute and reload.

If your prometheus shows the exporter as a Up you should also be able to see some metrics via the autocompletion if you navigate back to the prometheus start page and enter fritz into the search bar.

docs.title: Configuring Grafana
docs.text:
Now you can point your browser to http://localhost:3000/ to access Grafana. Login with username "admin" and password "admin" and set a new password (and make sure you do not forget that password). Once logged into Grafana open the menu and go to "Connections" -> "Data sources".

Click "Add new data source" and choose "Prometheus" from the list. Enter http://prometheus:9090 for the URL, leave everything else as is, scroll down and click on "Save & Test". You should see a green checkmark indicating that Grafana was able to connect to prometheus.

Download fritz-exporter-home.json and fritz-exporter-overview.json from misc/grafana in the repository, at the tag of your exporter version (see Grafana dashboards). In Grafana go to "Dashboards" -> "New" -> "Import", click "Upload dashboard JSON file" and pick one of the files.

Click "Import". At the top of the dashboard, pick your Prometheus data source and the device, and you should be greeted by a dashboard showing some data from your devices.

docs.title: plain Docker (docker run)
docs.text:
Docker images are automatically pushed to Docker Hub and are built for linux/amd64, linux/arm/v6, linux/arm/v7 and linux/arm64, the latter three being useful for e.g. Raspberry Pi type systems.

To run simply use

docker run -d -e FRITZ_USERNAME="prometheus" -e FRITZ_PASSWORD="monitoring" -p 9787:9787 --name fritz_exporter pdreker/fritz_exporter

This will use the default hostname of fritz.box for the device and name it after the hostname.

The image runs as user nobody (65534) and sets FRITZ_LISTEN_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0, so the published port reaches the exporter.

If you are monitoring multiple device you must use the config file method like this:

docker run -d -v /path/to/fritz-exporter.yaml:/app/fritz-exporter.yaml -p 9787:9787 --name fritz_exporter pdreker/fritz_exporter --config /app/fritz-exporter.yaml

/path/to/fritz-exporter.yaml is your local copy of the configuration, which will be mounted into the container. It must be readable by user nobody (65534), like a password_file, and it must set listen_address: 0.0.0.0: the environment variables do not apply when a config file is used, and the default 127.0.0.1 is not reachable from outside the container.

See the example config file provided at Config file.

docs.title: Config via environment variables
docs.text:
To run the exporter from docker-compose create an empty directory fritz-exporter and put a file docker-compose.yml in the directory (replace the environment variables with appropriate values) with the following content:

# Example file for running the exporter from the published image at hub.docker.com
services:
  fritz-exporter:
    image: pdreker/fritz_exporter:4
    container_name: fritz-exporter
    restart: always
    environment:
      FRITZ_HOSTNAME: 'fritz.box'
      FRITZ_USERNAME: 'prometheus'
      FRITZ_PASSWORD: 'prompassword'
    ports:
      - "9787:9787"

Then run docker compose up -d to start the exporter.

docs.title: Config via config file
docs.text:
Create an empty directory fritz-exporter and put a file docker-compose.yml in the directory (check the correct path for the config file) with the following content:

services:
  fritz-exporter:
    image: pdreker/fritz_exporter:4
    command: --config /fritz-exporter.yml
    container_name: fritz-exporter
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "9787:9787"
    volumes:
      - "/path/to/fritz-exporter.yml:/fritz-exporter.yml"

Create a config file for the exporter in this directory named fritz-exporter.yml. See the example config file provided at Config file. It must set listen_address: 0.0.0.0 and be readable by user nobody (65534), see above.

docs.title: Bare Metal (no container)
docs.text:
Running directly from sources is not recommended and should only be used for development. Please run this from docker/containers for real use.

This exporter requires Python 3.14 or later.

This project uses uv to manage dependencies. Install it, then recreate the virtual environment by running uv sync from the checked out repository.

The exporter can directly be run from a shell. Set the environment vars or config file as described in the configuration section of this README and run uv run python -m fritzexporter [--config /path/to/config/file.yaml] from the code directory.

docs.title: Systemd
docs.text:
It's also possible to run the exporter using a systemd service.

Make sure you have Python 3.14 or later and pip installed on your system. Usually these packages are called python3 and python3-pip. Please consult your distro documentation.

Create a new user for the exporter.

useradd --home-dir /opt/fritz-exporter \
        --create-home \
        --system \
        --shell /usr/sbin/nologin \
        fritz-exporter

Note: If you get a warning similar to useradd: Warning: missing or non-executable shell '/usr/sbin/nologin', thats completely normal!

Install fritzexporter using pip for the new user.

sudo --user=fritz-exporter \
   pip install --user \
       fritz-exporter \
       --no-warn-script-location

Now create the systemd service file at /etc/systemd/system/fritz-exporter.service with the following content:

fritz-exporter.service
[Unit]
After=network.target

[Service]
# These are security options which sandbox the service
LockPersonality=true
MemoryDenyWriteExecute=true
NoNewPrivileges=true
PrivateDevices=true
PrivateTmp=true
ProtectClock=true
ProtectControlGroups=true
ProtectHome=true
ProtectHostname=true
ProtectKernelLogs=true
ProtectKernelModules=true
ProtectKernelTunables=true
ProtectSystem=strict
RemoveIPC=true
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET6
RestrictNamespaces=true
RestrictRealtime=true
RestrictSUIDSGID=true
SystemCallArchitectures=native

# This gets run when the service starts up
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 -m fritzexporter --config /etc/fritz-exporter/config.yaml
User=fritz-exporter
Group=fritz-exporter
WorkingDirectory=/tmp
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Create your configuration file at /etc/fritz-exporter/config.yaml. See the example config file provided at Config file.

If you changed something in the fritz-exporter.service file, make sure to run systemctl daemon-reload afterwards, otherwise your changes won't get picked up.

# create configuration directory
mkdir -p /etc/fritz-exporter

# create configuration file using your favorite editor e.g. vim, nano
nano /etc/fritz-exporter/config.yaml

# Change owner and group of config to fritz-exporter
chown fritz-exporter:fritz-exporter /etc/fritz-exporter/config.yaml
# Change permissions to only allow the owner to read and write this file
chmod 600 /etc/fritz-exporter/config.yaml

Start and enable the service to start at boot.

systemctl start fritz-exporter.service
systemctl enable fritz-exporter.service

# Check the service status
systemctl status fritz-exporter.service

# View service logs
journalctl -fe -u fritz-exporter.service

docs.title: v4.0.0
docs.text: The first three sections need action from most users: dashboards and alerts that use the moved labels, configs without name, and Docker or Helm setups.

docs.title: Changing labels moved to _info metrics
docs.text:
Labels that change while the thing they describe stays the same made a new series each time, and for counters a reset: a Fritz!OS update, a reconnect, a mobile fallback, a new DHCP lease, a client roaming to the other band. They moved to a separate metric with the value 1, which you can join on its key labels.

  • Device: fritz_uptime_seconds_total loses modelname and softwareversion; they are in the new fritz_device_info.
  • Reachability: fritz_device_reachable is keyed by friendly_name only and loses serial. A device that was not reachable at startup was reported with serial="n/a" and got a new series once it came online. The serial number is in fritz_device_info.
  • Fritz!OS update: fritz_update_available loses newsoftwareversion; the new fritz_update_info{newsoftwareversion} has a series only while an update is available.
  • WAN access type: fritz_connection_mode loses access_type, and fritz_wan_max_bitrate_bps and fritz_wan_phys_link_status lose wantype (the same value); it is in the new fritz_wan_access_type_info{access_type}.
  • PPP: fritz_ppp_connection_state loses last_error; it is in the new fritz_ppp_connection_info.
  • WAN connections: fritz_wan_connection_uptime_seconds_total and fritz_wan_connection_status lose ip_address and state; both are in the new fritz_wan_connection_info{connection, connection_name, media_type, stack, state, ip_address}.
  • WiFi: fritz_wifi_status, fritz_wifi_channel, fritz_wifi_associations_count and fritz_wifi_packets_count_total are keyed by wifi_index and wifi_name only; ssid and standard are in the new fritz_wifi_info, and the enabled label is the new gauge fritz_wifi_enabled.
  • WiFi clients (wifi_client_info: true): fritz_wifi_client_signal_strength and fritz_wifi_client_speed are keyed by client_mac only; wifi_name and client_ip are in the new fritz_wifi_client_info.
  • Hosts (host_info: true): fritz_host_active and fritz_host_speed are keyed by mac_address only; ip_address, hostname, interface, port and model are in the new fritz_host_info. Hosts without a MAC address (e.g. some VPN clients) are left out, since nothing tells them apart.

To keep a label in a query, join the _info metric on its key labels, e.g.:

fritz_host_active * on (serial, mac_address) group_left (hostname) fritz_host_info
fritz_wifi_associations_count * on (serial, wifi_index) group_left (ssid) fritz_wifi_info

docs.title: Stricter configuration
docs.text:
The exporter now refuses to start, with one message that names the device and the key, on:

  • a key it does not know, at the top level or in a device (a typo such as pasword: used to be ignored, and the device then logged in without a password);
  • a device without password or password_file in the config file;
  • two devices with the same name. The name now defaults to the hostname, in the config file and for FRITZ_NAME; it used to be empty in the config file and Fritz!Box from the environment. Without a name, the friendly_name label of your series changes, so set name (or FRITZ_NAME) to keep it.
  • a password_file the exporter cannot read, or a password longer than 32 characters in it (a long password in password was refused already; from a file it only gave a warning);
  • a value of the wrong type for a text key, e.g. name: true. Numbers are taken as written (name: 7590 is "7590"); before, a number as name made every scrape fail.
  • a number with a fraction or a boolean for a number key, e.g. connection_timeout: 2.5 or port: true; these used to be cut to 2 and taken as 1.

A config file that is not valid YAML, or of the wrong shape, gives that message instead of a traceback; it names the line and column, not the text there.

docs.title: Docker image and Helm chart
docs.text:
• The image runs as user nobody (65534) instead of root. A mounted config file or password file must be readable by that user. The Helm chart already ran the container as 65534.
  • The image sets FRITZ_LISTEN_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0, so a published port reaches the exporter with the environment configuration. With a config file, set listen_address: 0.0.0.0 in it.
  • The Helm chart puts listen_address: 0.0.0.0 into the config secret it creates, unless config sets listen_address. A secret of your own (createConfigSecret: false) must set it.
  • The image installs the dependency versions from uv.lock, checked against their hashes.
  • The Helm chart takes the container port from config.exporter_port (default 9787) and uses service.portName for the container, the service and the ServiceMonitor; both used to be fixed to 9787 and metrics. A secret of your own that sets exporter_port needs config.exporter_port set to the same value.

docs.title: New Grafana dashboards
docs.text: misc/grafana now holds two dashboards built for 4.0, "Fritz!Exporter Overview" and "Fritz!Exporter Home" (see Grafana dashboards); the three earlier ones are gone from the repository. Dashboards of your own that use the moved labels need the _info metrics, see above.

docs.title: Legacy MD5 web login disabled by default
docs.text:
Devices on Fritz!OS before 7.24 only offer an MD5 login to the web interface, which the smart home, DOCSIS, fibre and REST API metrics use. The exporter now refuses that login by default: it logs an error and reads no web interface metrics from that device until it is restarted; its TR-064 metrics keep working. To get them back, upgrade Fritz!OS or set allow_unsafe_md5_password: true (env: FRITZ_ALLOW_UNSAFE_MD5_PASSWORD) for it. See Legacy MD5 web login.

Earlier versions did not ask the device for the PBKDF2 login, which Fritz!OS 7.24 and later only offer on request, and so used the MD5 login on every firmware. They now ask for it, so devices on Fritz!OS 7.24 and later log in with PBKDF2 without any change on your side.

After a refused web login (wrong credentials, or logins blocked by the device) the exporter now waits at least a minute, or as long as the device blocks logins, before the next attempt. It used to try again for every web interface metric group, which made the device block logins longer, also for the browser.

The exporter now logs in again only when the device rejects the session, not after every failed request or every 15 minutes, and it stops sending web interface requests for the rest of a scrape once the device does not answer one. A page the device refuses right after a login (the exporter's user lacks the right for it) gets a new login only every 15 minutes, so a right granted later takes effect; it used to cost a login on every scrape, each one an entry in the device's event log. Replies larger than 4 MiB are refused.

docs.title: --donate-data removed
docs.text: The data donation (--donate-data, --upload-data, --sanitize) is gone. To help with a device the exporter does not support yet, open an issue.

docs.title: Devices without a readable serial number are not collected
docs.text: The serial number is the label that tells devices apart in Prometheus. A device that answers but gives no readable serial number is now reported as unreachable (fritz_device_reachable 0) instead of being collected with serial="n/a". The exporter retries it three times, then gives up with an error in the log until it is restarted. A missing serial in the device's reply used to stop the exporter at startup.

docs.title: Only a device that does not answer is reported as unreachable
docs.text:
Any TR-064 error used to report the device as unreachable (fritz_device_reachable 0) for the scrape and drop the metrics collected after it, even when the device answered, e.g. with "action not supported". Now only a device that does not answer (refused, timed out, reset) is unreachable; an error reply skips the metric group that got it, shown in fritz_read_problem; one for a single host, WiFi client or similar skips only that one. A failure to fetch the mesh list only skips the mesh metrics. Two mesh links between nodes of the same names on the same interface would be two identical series, which made Prometheus refuse the whole scrape; the second is now skipped and reported, so give your mesh nodes different names.

host_info: true now also works on a device with fewer than two hosts in its host table; such a device used to fail its setup and was never collected.

docs.title: WAN byte counters no longer wrap at 4 GiB
docs.text: On Fritz!OS 7, fritz_wan_data_bytes_total came from 32-bit totals that wrap every 4 GiB, which Prometheus takes as a counter reset: traffic graphs read too low. The exporter now takes the 64-bit totals where the device has them (every WAN box seen so far). On such a box the counter jumps once after the upgrade, which shows as a single spike in rates.

docs.title: Offline devices are set up again in the background
docs.text: A scrape used to wait while the exporter tried to set up the devices that were offline, up to their connection timeout each. A background thread now does that, and the scrape returns at once; a device that comes back is collected from the next scrape on. The exporter also no longer runs a whole scrape at startup before it serves /metrics.

docs.title: Unreadable data is skipped and reported
docs.text: When a value, an item (a host, a channel, ...) or a whole reply cannot be read, the exporter skips only that part and reports it in the new fritz_read_problem metric and in the log. Before, such a value silently became a gap, or the whole scrape failed. See below for the new log messages.

docs.title: Unknown values are no longer reported as 0
docs.text:
• Fibre levels: some fibre boxes answer 0 for both optical levels over TR-064; the exporter then reads them from the web interface. When that fails, it used to export 0 dBm; now fritz_fiber_optical_signal_level_dBm and fritz_fiber_transmit_optical_level_dBm have no sample, and the failure shows in fritz_read_problem{capability="WanFiberInterfaceConfig",level="partial"} instead of a warning on every scrape.
  • DOCSIS channels without a channel ID used to be exported as channel 0, several of them as the same series; they are now skipped and reported.
  • A web interface reply without its data part (e.g. a docInfo page without data) used to give no metrics without a word; it is now reported as a read problem. An empty data part still means "no data".
  • Smart home: Fritz!OS leaves an element empty when the value is unknown. An empty <batterylow/> or <lock/> used to be exported as 0 ("battery fine", "not locked"); it now gives no sample for fritz_ha_battery_low or fritz_ha_switch_lock.
  • Thermostats switched off or on: Fritz!OS reports these as set temperature 253 and 254. They used to be exported as 126.5 °C and 127 °C in fritz_ha_heater_set_temperature_C (and the comfort and reduced temperatures); now there is no sample while a thermostat is switched off or on.

docs.title: Log messages reworked
docs.text:
Many log messages changed wording, level or frequency. If you match log messages, e.g. for alerts or in a log analysis tool, check your patterns. For alerting, consider the fritz_read_problem and fritz_device_reachable metrics instead, which do not depend on wording.

  • Device names: every message about a device names it the same way, "\<name> (\<host>)", e.g. "Fritz!Box 7690 (fritz.box)", or the host alone if the name is the host. Messages used to show the host, the serial number ("device serial …") or no device at all.
  • Skipped data (replaces "Failed to fetch … data from …"):
    • "Could not read \<Capability> data from \<device>, skipping it: \<reason>" — the whole capability was skipped for this scrape;
    • "Skipped part of the \<Capability> data from \<device>: \<details>" — some values or items were skipped;
    • "Bug while collecting \<Capability> data from \<device>, …" — an error in the exporter, logged at ERROR with a traceback;
    • while a problem lasts, the warning is repeated once an hour as "…, still since \<time> (\<n> scrapes): …" instead of on every scrape (details at DEBUG in between), and "Reading \<Capability> data from \<device> works again" is logged at INFO when it is gone.
  • Devices that stay offline: "Device \<device> is still offline, now because: \<reason>" at WARNING when the reason changes, and "Giving up on device \<device>: its serial number could not be read \<n> times: …" at ERROR. An unexpected error while setting up a device is logged with its traceback and "(unexpected; please report this)", and keeps only that device offline.
  • Web login: "login not retried for \<n> seconds after: \<reason>" while the exporter waits after a refused login.
  • Devices that cannot be set up: one error, "Failed to initialize device \<device>, it will be reported as down: \<reason>", without a traceback. It replaces "unable to connect to …", "Not authorized to get device info from …" (the reason now ends in "(check username and password)") and "Device \<device> has no detected capabilities." (now a reason, and the exporter keeps running).
  • Unreachable during a scrape: "Device \<device> is unreachable, skipping \<Capability> metrics for this collection cycle: \<reason>" at WARNING, without a traceback.

docs.title: Remote access uses one port for TR-064 and the web interface
docs.text:
With remote_access: true (env: FRITZ_REMOTE_ACCESS), port now sets the remote HTTPS port for both TR-064 and the web interface (smart home, DOCSIS, fibre and REST API metrics). Without port the exporter now uses 443 for both; it used to send TR-064 to 49443, which the device does not serve over remote access.

Local scrapes are not affected: port still sets only the TR-064 port there. See Ports, TLS and remote access.

docs.title: Smart home (AHA) metrics now work over local TLS
docs.text: With use_tls: true the exporter used to send smart home requests to the device's remote access port, which fails on the LAN. When that happened it also reported the device as unreachable and skipped the metrics collected after smart home. It now sends them to port 443, and a failed smart home fetch no longer marks the device unreachable.

docs.title: Default connection timeout added
docs.text:
connection_timeout (env: FRITZ_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT) now defaults to 10 seconds instead of no timeout. The timeout is used for the initial TR-064 connection as well as every HTTP read done during a scrape (including smart-home AHA calls), so a slow or wedged device can no longer block the exporter indefinitely.

Setting connection_timeout: 0 restores the previous behaviour (no timeout).

Why: the exporter used to block a scrape forever on a device that stopped responding. Parallel scrapes (e.g. multiple Prometheus instances) would then accumulate behind that stuck scrape and all stop receiving metrics until the exporter was restarted. The new default bounds this so scrapes complete and report the device as unreachable.

docs.title: Default listen address changed
docs.text:
The default value of listen_address (env: FRITZ_LISTEN_ADDRESS) has changed from 0.0.0.0 to 127.0.0.1.

Who is affected: deployments that rely on the old default to expose the exporter on all network interfaces — for example, a bare-metal install where Prometheus scrapes the exporter over the network without an explicit listen_address setting.

Who is not affected: Docker/Kubernetes deployments that publish the port at the container/pod level; any deployment that already sets FRITZ_LISTEN_ADDRESS or listen_address explicitly in the config file.

What to do: if you need the exporter to be reachable from another host, set listen_address: 0.0.0.0 in your config file or FRITZ_LISTEN_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0 in your environment explicitly. Closes #402.

docs.title: Home automation metric label change
docs.text:
All fritz_ha_* Prometheus metrics now include a populated device_id label. Previously this label was always emitted as an empty string "" due to a bug; it now carries the real NewDeviceId value from the Fritz!Box.

Impact: Prometheus treats a changed label set as a new time series. On the first scrape after upgrading, all existing fritz_ha_* series will be replaced by new ones, causing counter resets. Any dashboards or alerts that filtered on {device_id=""} will stop matching.

What to do: update dashboards and alert rules to either remove the device_id filter or match the real device ID value. Counter-based panels may show a reset spike on the first scrape; this is expected and will stabilise on the next collection cycle.

docs.title: Label changes
docs.text:
Version 2.0.0 changes the direction labels of some metrics to consistently use tx (transmitted, upstream) and rx (received, downstream). Before this change the labels were up and down respectively, while other metrics used tx and rx.

Affected metrics:

  • fritz_wan_data
  • fritz_wan_data_packets

docs.title: Config changes
docs.text: Multi device configuration was dropped from the environment configuration. The FRITZ_EXPORTER_CONFIG environment variable was removed completely. When using environment configuration this exporter now only supports a single device. For multi device support please use the new config file option.

docs.title: WiFi metrics changes
docs.text: All WiFi metrics have been merged. So e.g. fritz_wifi_2_4GHz_* is changed to fritz_wifi_* and two labels (wifi_index and wifi_name) are added to the metrics.

docs.title: v1.0.0
docs.text:
Version 1.0.0 of the exporter has completely reworked how this exports metrics! If you have used this exporter in the past, you will get a completely new set of metrics.

  • the metrics prefix has changed from fritzbox_ to fritz_
  • all labels have been converted to lower-case (e.g. Serial -> serial) to be in line with the common usage of labels
  • some metrics have been renamed to better reflect their content
